title: Given an m by n board of characters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed by sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically neighboring), where each cell is used at most once per word.
shortTitle: Word Search II: Trie + DFS backtracking on grid

s1_definition.oneliner: Build one Trie from all dictionary words, DFS the grid with backtracking while walking the Trie, and collect words at end-of-word nodes.
s1_definition.profdef:
Word Search II combines a Trie data structure with grid DFS backtracking.

- **Trie construction** inserts all dictionary words so shared prefixes are tested together.
- **DFS with Trie pointer** walks the grid and advances the Trie pointer in lock-step.
- **Prefix pruning** stops any path whose prefix no dictionary word shares, avoiding dead-end exploration.
- **Word collection** stores the complete word on the terminal Trie node for O(1) retrieval.
- **Leaf pruning** optionally removes Trie nodes after a word is found to shrink the tree during search.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a grid of letters on a fraud-detection heat map and a watchlist of suspicious code words. Instead of hunting for each watchlist word separately, you build one big index of all the words and sweep the grid once. At each cell you check the index: if the letters walked so far are not the start of any watchlist word, you abandon that path immediately.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Trie for words ["oath", "oat", "eat"]:

       root
       ├── o
       │   └── a
       │       └── t  (word: "oat")
       │           └── h  (word: "oath")
       └── e
           └── a
               └── t  (word: "eat")

  DFS on Grid with Trie:

  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┐
  │ o │ a │ a │ n │   Trie pointer starts at root
  ├───┼───┼───┼───┤   Cell 'o' -> root has child 'o' -> advance
  │ e │ t │ a │ e │   Cell 'a' -> 'o' has child 'a' -> advance
  ├───┼───┼───┼───┤   Cell 't' -> 'a' has child 't' -> advance
  │ i │ h │ k │ r │   node.word = "oat" -> COLLECT
  ├───┼───┼───┼───┤   Cell 'h' -> 't' has child 'h' -> advance
  │ i │ f │ l │ v │   node.word = "oath" -> COLLECT
  └───┴───┴───┴───┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search II asks for every dictionary word that can be traced through adjacent cells of a grid, each cell used at most once per word. The naive approach runs a separate grid search for each word, which repeats enormous amounts of work. My efficient solution builds one Trie from all the words so their shared prefixes are tested together, then sweeps the grid a single time with a depth-first backtracking search that walks a Trie pointer in lock-step with the grid path.

Before stepping into a cell, I check whether its character is a child of the current Trie node, and if not I abandon the path immediately. This pruning is the whole reason the single-Trie approach wins. When the Trie pointer reaches a node whose stored word field is set, I collect that word and clear the field so the same word is not reported twice. I mark the cell visited before recursing into its four neighbors and restore it on the way back.

The details interviewers look for are sharing one Trie across all words rather than one per word, storing the full word string on the terminal node for constant-time collection, and the correct mark-and-restore to enforce the use-each-cell-once rule per path.

In my project at National Bank of India, I applied this to a fraud-pattern grid where flagged activity is encoded as a character matrix and compliance keeps a watchlist of coded patterns. Building one Trie from the whole watchlist let me find every embedded pattern in a single sweep.

Remember one sentence: build one Trie from all words, DFS the grid with a Trie pointer, prune dead prefixes, and collect words at terminal nodes.

---

keyPoints: Build one Trie from all dictionary words to test shared prefixes together in a single grid sweep
DFS walks a Trie pointer in lock-step with the grid path, pruning any prefix no word shares
Store the complete word string on the terminal Trie node for O(1) collection
Clear the word field after collection to prevent duplicate reporting of the same word
Mark grid cells visited with a sentinel and restore on backtrack to enforce use-once-per-path
Worst-case time is O(m*n*4^L) but Trie pruning makes practical cost much smaller
Leaf pruning removes exhausted Trie branches during search to speed up remaining exploration
